name: list

density.note: one statement per line, not a paragraph

description: Bulleted list under a heading — plain pills, hairline takeaways, or display-weight principles.
purpose: Use when the items are genuinely a flat list of one-line points. The default renders accent-bordered pills; the `takeaway` variant renders hairline-ruled single-line takeaways (former tldr); the `principles` variant renders display-weight numbered statements with a large counter (former principles). For richer per-item structure, prefer cards-grid, cards-stack, or list-tabular.

items.description: List items. Keep each under ~12 words.

skeleton:
<!-- _class: list -->

## Slide heading.

- First short bullet point.
- Second short bullet point.
- Third short bullet point.
- Fourth short bullet point.
- Fifth short bullet point.
sample:
<!-- _class: list -->

## The list states one point per line.

- A line is a complete statement, not a fragment.
- Fourteen words is the budget a line may spend.
- Six lines fill the canvas comfortably.
- Parallel openings keep the scan honest.
- Nesting belongs to card layouts, not here.

stressDoc.caption: Eight lines at the hard ceiling.
stressDoc.sample:
<!-- _class: list -->

## Eight lines is the most a list should carry.

- A stress line may spend twenty words, and this one spends them to show where the wrap lands.
- Even at the ceiling every line stays one complete statement with a single clause of support.
- The third line is where a reading audience starts skimming instead.
- Vary sentence length or eight dense lines blur into one.
- The fifth line should carry something worth the fatigue.
- Numbers and names hold attention better than abstractions here.
- The seventh line is the last one anyone quotes.
- Eight is the stop; nine becomes a memo.

whenToUse.title: Genuinely a list
whenToUse.body: Five to six short points, each under twelve words. No internal structure per item — just a heading and the bullets.

whenToUse.title: Numbered when order matters
whenToUse.body: Use `ol` (`1.` source) when sequence is load-bearing; `ul` when order is interchangeable. Numbers render as a tabular leading column.

whenToUse.title: Pills via inline code
whenToUse.body: Inline code at the end of a row becomes a pill (status tag, metric, owner). Lets the list double as a lightweight ledger without changing layout.

whenToUse.title: Takeaways at a section close
whenToUse.body: The `takeaway` variant renders each item as a hairline-ruled single line at message weight — the deck or section's headline points. Add `numbered` for a large accent counter. (Absorbed the standalone `tldr` component on 2026-06-07.)

whenToUse.title: Declared principles or tenets
whenToUse.body: The `principles` variant renders an ordered list of single-sentence declarations at display weight with a large accent counter. Compose `lettered`, `roman`, or `bullet` to switch the counter format. (Absorbed the standalone `principles` component on 2026-06-07.)

antiPatterns.title: Title plus body per item
antiPatterns.body: If each bullet is `**Title.** body`, the layout under-serves it. Move to cards-stack (2-3 items) or list-tabular (5+ rows) instead.

antiPatterns.title: Wall of long bullets
antiPatterns.body: Past twelve words per line the slide becomes paragraph soup. Either trim or move to content for prose, cards-stack for structured items.

antiPatterns.title: Two-item lists
antiPatterns.body: Two bullets read as a thin slide. For pairs, reach for compare-prose — it gives the pair the weight it deserves.

related.name: cards-stack
related.when: each item has a title plus body sentence

related.name: list-tabular
related.when: five or more rows with label-plus-description

related.name: checklist
related.when: items carry state markers (done / partial / todo)

takeaway.label: takeaway
takeaway.caption: Ruled single lines for conclusions.
takeaway.sample:
<!-- _class: list takeaway -->

## takeaway boxes the list as findings.

- The box frames the lines as conclusions.
- Lead with the strongest finding.
- Five lines read as a verdict.
- Longer sets go back to plain list.

principles.label: principles
principles.caption: Numbered declarations at display weight.
principles.sample:
<!-- _class: list principles -->

## principles numbers the house rules.

1. State each rule as an imperative.
2. Keep rules under ten words.
3. Order them by how often they apply.
4. Retire a rule you keep breaking.

numbered.label: numbered
numbered.caption: Accent counters on the takeaway box.
numbered.sample:
<!-- _class: list takeaway numbered -->

## numbered ranks the boxed findings.

- Ranks turn findings into priorities.
- The top line owns the meeting.
- Three ranked lines beat six flat ones.

lettered.label: lettered
lettered.caption: Letters replace the counters.
lettered.sample:
<!-- _class: list principles lettered -->

## lettered counts the rules with letters.

1. Letters read as options, not sequence.
2. Use them when order is arbitrary.
3. Three options is a decision; six is a menu.

roman.label: roman
roman.caption: Roman numerals replace counters.
roman.sample:
<!-- _class: list principles roman -->

## roman sets the rules in numerals.

1. Numerals lend formal weight.
2. Reserve them for charters and mandates.
3. Past five, the gravitas becomes parody.

bullet.label: bullet
bullet.caption: Dots replace the counters.
bullet.sample:
<!-- _class: list principles bullet -->

## bullet strips the markers back to dots.

1. Dots drop the counting entirely.
2. The principles frame stays.
3. Use when rules are peers.
